title: Characterization and Monte Carlo Simulation of Wavelength-Shifting Absorption Length in Plastic Optical Fibers
abstract: We report an experimental characterization of the wavelength-shifting (WLS) absorption length of the EJ-160I fiber core material from Eljen Technology. Fiber-core samples of different thicknesses were employed, and the transmitted intensity of incident LED light was measured to extract the WLS absorption length at 405.7 nm. The resulting value, (0.823 +/- 0.038) mm, was used to normalize the WLS absorption length spectrum derived from the absorption spectrum of the core material. An independent measurement at 392.5 nm yielded a WLS absorption length of (1.404 +/- 0.074) mm, differing from the value predicted by the reconstructed WLS absorption length spectrum by 3.16%, corresponding to 0.43 sigma. The resulting spectrum was implemented as an optical input in a Geant4-based optical Monte Carlo simulation of the EJ-160I fiber to examine the role of the WLS absorption length in light output, light attenuation, and the emission spectrum.

title: Towards Automatic Ion Identification in Storage Rings
abstract: Resonant Schottky detectors provide non-destructive, single-ion-sensitive measurements of revolution frequencies and intensities of ion species stored in a heavy-ion storage ring. These high-\(Q\) cavities allow analysis of high-order harmonics of the revolution frequencies to magnify absolute frequency separations. Adjacent harmonic ranges can, however, overlap within the detector band, making frequency alone insufficient for determining the ion's mass-to-charge ratio $(m/q)$. We present a proof-of-concept for an automated harmonic de-overlapping method using spectral shapes in combined Schottky and Isochronous Mass Spectrometry. The empirical ansatz is that, for a fixed ion-optical setting, each peak, corresponding to a specific ion species with given $m/q$ ratio, has a characteristic profile that evolves smoothly with changing $m/q$. Occurrences of the same local structure at different harmonics should therefore retain almost identical shapes after frequency rescaling. Applied to a 245\,MHz spectrum accumulated from 11\,452 injections at the Experimental Storage Ring at GSI, the method organizes 16 of 32 detected structures into five candidate families and reconstructs their fundamental-frequency representation. Reducing the complex mixed-harmonic spectrum to this smaller candidate set solves the challenging task of finding initial anchors for the ion identification.

title: HEP-like 1550 nm wide-field pixelated optical receiver for inter-satellite laser links: a simulation-based proof of concept for Earth, lunar and Earth-Moon scenarios
abstract: I propose and evaluate by simulation a wide-field dome optical receiver (a field of view larger than a hemisphere) at 1550 nm for the acquisition of inter-satellite laser links. The detector is an InGaAs pixel hybrid of about 1 Mpixel with event-driven, time-stamped readout, inspired by the pixel detectors of high-energy physics. A pulsed beacon is detected by the coincidence of m hits in a sliding block of pixels, and the angle of arrival (AoA) is estimated by clustering and centroiding and handed to a narrow-field data channel. In a 550 km Earth constellation, with a 5 mrad beacon and a 10 mm aperture, detection takes 12 $\mu$s to 2 ms (up to 116 ms with the 6-9 mm that the optics allow), with a whole-frame false-alarm rate below 0.01/s, and the AoA error is 0.13-0.23 mrad. Cooling to about 233 K gives a service life above 5 years for fluences up to about $2\times10^{9}$ p/cm$^2$ per year. The receiver is also studied around the Moon and on the Earth-Moon link, where it works only between high orbits. Compared phase by phase with published scan-based acquisition, the search phase (3-18 ms with 10 mm) is shorter by a factor of about $10^{2}$ to $10^{5}$; end to end, with assumed pointing and loop-closure times, it takes 0.16-1.5 s, comparable to a terminal with calibrated open-loop pointing but without requiring that pointing at the receiver; the partner's beacon must still be pointed at it to about 1.25 mrad (5 mrad beacon). All values are simulation results, obtained with idealised optics and a 1 Mpixel detector that does not exist today; none is a measurement.

title: Design and performance of a top-loading vibrating-sample magnetometer for a helium-flow variable-temperature insert
abstract: We present a custom-built top-loading probe that adds vibrating-sample magnetometry to an existing helium-flow variable-temperature insert without replacing its cryogenic or magnetic-field infrastructure. The modular instrument combines a detachable sealed drive head, a voice-coil resonator operating near 44 Hz, continuous monitoring of the peak vibration amplitude, motorized axial centering, and a compact first-order pickup-coil gradiometer. A numerical flux-linkage calculation reproduces the position and shape of the measured axial response for several vibration amplitudes after multiplication by a common factor of 1.08. Measurements on Ni reference samples demonstrate operation down to 5 K and yield effective geometrical factors between 24.0 V s A$^{-1}$ m$^{-3}$ and 31.4 V s A$^{-1}$ m$^{-3}$. At fixed field, the observed voltage scatter corresponds to moment-equivalent one-standard-deviation repeatabilities of 16.5 nA m$^{2}$ to 27.8 nA m$^{2}$. For a 31.7 nm Ni film measured at 250 K, magnetization curves obtained at three vibration amplitudes approximately collapse after amplitude correction and yield a saturation magnetization of approximately 409 kA m$^{-1}$ after subtraction of the linear high-field background. The results demonstrate a practical retrofit approach for adding bulk and thin-film magnetometry to VTIs with comparable bore and flange constraints.

title: A Multimode-Fiber Speckle Sensing Node with a Press-Robust Quantized Network for Liquid-Cooling Thermal Monitoring
abstract: Liquid-cooled AI and HPC racks concentrate heat at cold plates and manifolds, below the granularity of facility sensors. We present a self-contained edge node that turns one multimode fiber into a distributed thermal-event sensor over nine pipe segments, with a 450 nm laser, a camera and a Zynq UltraScale+ device that captures, infers, displays and reports over MQTT. The speckle decorrelates within tens of seconds at constant temperature, and a press can change it as much as a 1 degree Celsius rise. The node averages each 20 s window and feeds two planes, the mean pattern and a 19-dimensional temporal-feature map, to a 61.6k-parameter int8 convolutional neural network (CNN) that treats presses as hard negatives and runs in the programmable logic at 565 microseconds per frame. On a 59-session, 70,148-window dataset, session-held-out validation gives a pooled AUC of 0.961 against 0.876 for decorrelation, no alarm during the hold or the 45 s rebound in 23 press trials against 6 and 16, and a mean per-fold step detection of 83.8% at 0.4 false alarms per hour.

title: In-pixel lock-in readout for wide-field nitrogen-vacancy radio-frequency spectrum analysis
abstract: The growing use of radio-frequency (RF) technologies requires compact, room-temperature sensors that can analyze a wide RF band in real time. Here we present a quantum RF spectrum analyzer based on the gradient-encoded electron spin resonance of a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) ensemble in diamond and read out with a $512\times542$-pixel lock-in camera that demodulates the signal in each pixel. On/off keying the signal under test at the camera's reference frequency lets every pixel extract the spin-resonant photoluminescence modulation. Before digitization, each pixel suppresses the static background and low-frequency noise that limit conventional camera readout. Translating a single permanent magnet tunes the encoded band continuously from 10~MHz to 32~GHz. The magnet position establishes a trade-off between instantaneous bandwidth (up to 4~GHz) and frequency resolution (7--22~MHz), with a 5~ms readout time. The wide-field readout integrates all spectral channels in parallel in a room-temperature sensor head and requires no phase synchronization to the RF carrier. The SNR remains above 70 at an applied power as low as $-32.5$~dBm. The magnetic-field configuration can be adapted to different RF bands without changing the pixel-parallel readout.

title: lawless: Normalization, Scaling, and Merging of Laue Data in the AIMLESS Framework
abstract: lawless, a new program for wavelength normalization, scaling, and merging of Laue data from both X-rays and neutrons, is presented. Based on the AIMLESS program, lawless provides two methods of wavelength normalization via Chebyshev polynomials and Gaussian process regression, the latter of which is a more general method for various sources. Coupled with AIMLESS gentler outlier rejection methodology and superior error modelling, lawless provides better quality neutron maps than previous methods by focusing on completeness over better-looking merging statistics. Even as R-factors increase and CC1/2 numbers decrease, dataset completeness is the biggest limiting factor in neutron map quality and should be a primary focus in data reduction.

title: Label-free self-calibration of a segmented HPGe $\gamma$-ray tracking array from the Compton scattering constraint
abstract: Pulse-shape analysis in segmented HPGe $\gamma$-ray tracking arrays such as AGATA relies on reference signals for known interaction positions, which are costly to measure and only approximate when calculated. In a simulation of 51 AGATA crystals, we show that the interaction positions can be learned from the pulses without position labels. For a \Co\ photon that is Compton scattered in one segment and absorbed in another, the scattering angle follows both from the deposited energies and from the positions of the source and of the two interactions. A neural network shared by all crystals predicts one position per fired segment and is trained only to make these two angles agree; the unmeasured order of the two interactions and the selection of the pairs are revised during training. The pulses, synthesised from AGATAGeFEM bases for $2.79\times10^{6}$ pairs of fired segments whose energies add up to a \Co\ line, selected from $4\times10^{7}$ simulated decays, include noise, cross-talk, trigger-time jitter and differences between crystals. For the hits of held-out pairs, the mean three-dimensional position error falls from 10.4~mm with the segment centres to 1.65~mm, with a FWHM of 1.0--1.3~mm in each coordinate, compared with 1.07~mm for the same network trained on the simulated positions. The constraint determines the positions along the crystal axes only weakly, and at small scattering angles it pulls low-energy first interactions towards the source, which is why deposits below 200~keV are excluded. Even with the simulated positions, the two angles differ, mainly because a segment with several interactions is described by a single position and energy rather than because of Doppler broadening.

title: Machine-learning-assisted photon pairing for neutral-pion reconstruction at future Higgs factories
abstract: Neutral-pion ($\pi^0$) reconstruction is important for precision measurements at high-energy colliders, particularly in flavor, $\tau$, and Higgs physics. We study $\pi^0$ candidate selection in four benchmark physics processes at electron--positron colliders, comparing an optimized diphoton mass-window (MW) baseline with four machine-learning methods: a boosted decision tree (BDT), a multilayer perceptron (MLP), ParticleNet (PN), and Particle Transformer (ParT). Performance is evaluated using the product of selection efficiency and purity. At the reference ECAL energy resolution, all four machine-learning methods outperform MW. PN and ParT achieve relative improvements of 53%--95% and 60%--128%, respectively, primarily through better rejection of incorrectly matched photon pairs. Their performance advantage is maintained across the investigated ECAL energy resolutions. Training-sample-size scans reveal two periods of rapid performance improvement separated by slower growth in most PN and ParT learning curves. The improved candidate selection provides a starting point for further studies of $\rho$ and hadronic $\tau$ reconstruction.

title: CHARMS250V1: A Cryogenic Front-End ASIC for Low-Noise Readout of Charge or Light Signals in Noble Liquid Detectors
abstract: This work presents the design and measurement results of CHARMS250V1, a next-generation cryogenic front-end application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) developed using a 65 nm CMOS process. It is designed for low-noise readout of charge or light signals generated in noble liquid detectors. CHARMS250V1 is a single channel prototype whose design in the future will be integrated within a 16-channel ASIC. It comprises pre-amplification and pulse shaping stages that provide programmable charge gain between 4.3 mV/fC and 25 mV/fC, peaking time programmable between 250 ns and 2 us, and programmable baseline of either 200 mV or 900 mV for processing of unipolar and bipolar signals, respectively.

title: Real-time event-level zero-shot learning at 150 ns: towards a foundation model for particle physics experiment triggering
abstract: The hardware-based Level-1 triggers of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments select collisions with algorithms designed for one signature each, acting on a coarse, low-latency view of every event. We present a learned event embedding for several trigger tasks and evaluate its transfer to processes absent from training. Using paired offline and Level-1 views of the same simulated collisions, we train an offline transformer with a supervised metric loss and distil it, event by event, into a quantised Level-1 transformer whose bit widths are learned under a fixed resource budget. Trained on 25 Standard Model processes, the embedding places 28 held-out processes next to their physical relatives. A nearest-neighbour selection against background collisions, which never enter encoder training, rejects 99% of them. It retains a median of 90% of seen and 96% of unseen Standard Model events and 88% of a set of 52 beyond-the-Standard-Model benchmark samples, the best-performing score across the three groups among the baselines evaluated on the same events. A second gate against the seen processes isolates high-mass dilepton signals into label-free clusters, and long-lived signals too when displaced-track information is available. With 7512 parameters and an FPGA latency of 147 ns, the encoder uses one event representation, learned once, to derive several selections, opening the door to a foundation model for the LHC's hardware-based triggers.

title: A high-speed and high-resolution 3D velocity map imaging system with a neuromorphic camera
abstract: An improved camera-based 3D-velocity map imaging (VMI) system was demonstrated with a neuromorphic camera. We show a machine vision event-driven camera can achieve an unprecedented latency of 2 microseconds when detecting single ion/electron with a microchannel plate imaging detector, which boosts the speed of the momentum imaging system to more than 100 kHz, while the system with a conventional frame camera is limited to a few kHz. The high spatial resolution of the camera offers additional performance boost while maintaining excellent multi-hit capability and a high time resolution.

title: Ion Backflow Suppression and Absorption Dynamics in Cascaded GEM Structures
abstract: Ion backflow (IBF) is a persistent challenge in Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) detectors: positive ions drifting back into the sensitive volume distort the drift field and degrade both spatial and energy resolution. We investigate the ion-absorption characteristics of single- to quintuple-GEM detectors using ANSYS and Garfield$^{++}$ for an Ar/CO$_2$ (70:30) gas mixture. A layer-resolved formalism is developed that distinguishes conditional foil-level absorption from a detector-level absorption metric that correctly weights ion production at every amplification stage. For the conventional biconical geometry, cascading foils improves the overall ion-absorption fraction only moderately, from 47.83\% for a single GEM to 59.06\% for a quintuple GEM. Replacing the biconical holes with a single-conical profile raises the absorption fraction to 75\%-87\% across the same range of multiplicities and reduces the IBF/Gain ratio by a factor of two to three an improvement that exceeds what is gained by adding four additional biconical foils. As a secondary test under more realistic conditions, the second transfer-gap length of a triple-GEM detector is varied from 1.2 to 3.5~mm. The gain shows a non-monotonic dependence with a maximum near 2.0-2.5~mm, while the IBF/Gain ratio decreases monotonically with increasing gap length; the single-conical geometry retains its factor-of-two advantage throughout. These findings establish that ion suppression in cascaded GEM structures is governed not only by the number of foils but primarily by the local ion-collection properties of each foil, and that single-conical holes represent a promising route to improved performance in high-rate detector applications.

title: Data handling, production, and simulation in the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab
abstract: This paper details the computing strategies of the Muon g-2 Experiment at Fermilab, which measured the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with a precision of 127 ppb by processing over 10 petabytes of detector and simulation data. This paper discusses the computational and operational challenges of data production, data handling, and data analysis of such large datasets. These challenges were overcome by using Fermilab-developed software infrastructure and production tools, making efficient use of resources, and improving the collaboration-developed reconstruction workflow. By overcoming these challenges, the experiment improved the data throughput capacity and reduced the analysis turnaround time by an order of magnitude over the course of its lifetime.

title: Efficient phase-only wavefront shaping at 250 kHz for multimode fiber endomicroscopy
abstract: Wavefront shaping through multimode fibers (MMFs) enables diffraction-limited fluorescence imaging with hair-thin probes, at a speed and light budget bounded by the wavefront modulator. Existing modulators provide at most two of three key characteristics: high refresh rate, (high) modal dimensionality, and light efficiency. Here, we demonstrate wavefront control through an MMF using a tailored phase-only microelectromechanical modulator that combines all three, with 8,192 elements arranged in a 32 x 256 array, 7-bit phase control, and a 250 kHz full-frame refresh rate. Direct on-axis phase modulation delivers 70+/-5% of the incident light into the modulated field and eliminates both off-axis encoding optical losses and hologram computation. The generated foci at the distal end of the fiber remain isotropic with high fidelity. We use singular-value decomposition analysis of the measured transmission to identify the effective degrees of freedom of our system. By scanning the focus at multiple depths, we demonstrate volumetric fluorescence imaging. These results open a new operating regime for adaptive in vivo multimode-fiber endoscopy.

title: A Camera-Based Single-Volume, Monolithic Compton Camera
abstract: A Compton camera measures two events in a detector from individual gamma-rays to reconstruct the radiation source. Conventional scintillator-based Compton cameras consist of two separate scintillator volumes or a single segmented scintillator, resulting in drawbacks regarding detector bulkiness and efficiency. Their scintillator readout techniques struggle to resolve two nearby events in one monolithic scintillator. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras have recently been proposed for measuring scintillation events in various configurations. SPAD array sensors enable high-resolution photon-counting acquisition at high rates that is easily scalable to millions of pixels. Prior work has explored different optics and measurement arrangements as well as demonstrated measurement of single interaction locations. In this work, we extend these capabilities to demonstrate a practical radiation imaging device in the form of a Compton camera consisting of a SPAD camera and one compact, monolithic scintillator. Our Compton camera prototype successfully reconstructs a gamma-ray source over multiple locations that span a 4$\pi$ steradian field of view. Our approach is able to resolve two simultaneous events in one monolithic scintillator and enables Compton camera devices with compact, monolithic scintillator volumes for enhanced portability.

title: Simulation and Rejection of Radon Progeny Backgrounds in nEXO
abstract: Radon-induced backgrounds from $^{214}$Bi decays remain a significant challenge for liquid xenon (LXe) detectors searching for neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$). We present a simulation-based study of the $^{214}$Bi background in nEXO, incorporating a physically motivated model of the transport and implantation of radon progeny into the detector cathode. We show that the spatial distribution of scintillation light provides an additional method for background discrimination for events surviving standard energy, event topology, and fiducial volume selections. A simple discriminator based on the scintillation light detected below the cathode rejects 41% of the remaining $^{214}$Bi backgrounds while retaining 95% of $0\nu\beta\beta$ signal events, and a convolutional neural network classifier improves this rejection to 57% at the same signal efficiency. An updated optical model provides a more accurate estimate of the light collection efficiency below the cathode than used in previous work, increasing the expected $^{214}$Bi-$^{214}$Po (Bi-Po) coincidence-tagging efficiency for bottom-surface $^{214}$Bi decays from less than 1% to approximately 50%. Together, these results demonstrate improved rejection of cathode-implanted $^{214}$Bi backgrounds in nEXO through complementary prompt scintillation-based discrimination and delayed coincidence tagging.

title: Ultrabroadband, high-sensitivity time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy enabled by a Yb-based laser system
abstract: Ultrafast optical fields have introduced numerous novel light-induced states in quantum materials. Identifying these states and elucidating their formation mechanisms require comprehensive, quantitative access to nonequilibrium electrodynamics across relevant energy scales. Here, we develop a Yb-laser-based time-resolved terahertz spectroscopy (TRTS) platform combining multi-pass-cell pulse compression, spintronic terahertz generation, and air-biased coherent detection. A single time-domain waveform scan provides continuous phase-resolved spectral coverage to 25 THz ($\sim$100 meV) with a Fourier resolution of 0.1 THz ($\sim$0.4 meV). This capability enables the characterization of both low-frequency charge dynamics and higher-energy resonant excitations in quantum materials under a common temporal reference. The system achieves a single-scan time-domain signal-to-noise ratio of 72 dB with long-term waveform stability, while preserving most of the laser pulse energy for tunable excitation. Measurements on intrinsic GaAs resolve extremely weak phonon features above 23 THz and demonstrate quantitative retrieval of equilibrium and transient complex optical properties. The resulting platform can provide a more complete microscopic picture of light-induced states in quantum materials.

title: Development of a Hybrid Scintillator Strip-Drift Tube Muon Detector for the FCC-ee
authors: Jiajin Ge (on behalf of the University of Michigan FCC-ee R&D team)
abstract: The Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee) is a proposed high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ collider for precision measurements at the electroweak, Higgs, and top-quark energy scales. A high-performance, cost-effective muon system is essential for muon identification, triggering, momentum measurement, and long-lived particle detection. We present the R&D of a hybrid muon detector concept combining fast extruded plastic scintillator strips with precision drift tubes. The scintillator strips were produced at Fermilab, while detector prototypes with SiPM readout and pressurized drift tubes were designed, constructed, and integrated at the University of Michigan. The hybrid detector was tested at the CERN test beam facility in 2025 and 2026. The scintillator strips achieved a position resolution of 1.6 mm and a time resolution of approximately 350 ps, while the drift tubes provided a single-hit spatial resolution better than 100 $\mu$m. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a high-performance hybrid muon spectrometer for the FCC-ee.

title: Ballistic propagation-mediated super-resolution light-element imaging: in-situ tracking dynamic hydrogen migration
abstract: Transmission electrons - with few-picometer wavelengths - can theoretically resolve all atoms in solids. However, constrained by factors such as lens aberrations, Z-contrast dependence and poor temporal resolution, the scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) fails to tackle the long-standing challenge of hydrogen dynamics on atomic scale. Here, our experiment-guided simulations reveal that unlike heavy-atom imaging - governed by wave-based imaging process - ballistic propagation of particle-like electrons in Cs-corrected TEM enables super-resolution imaging (SRI) of light atoms, achieving a resolution down to 14 pm and a robust hydrogen contrast of ~24%. Our in-situ SRI study not only uncovers polymetric hydrogen aggregation in TiHx and H-LaAlO3, but also inter-site migration, rotational displacement of hydrogen species and collective hydrogen tunneling-induced polarization surge in the oxide. By exploiting the novel electron-matter interactions, our findings offer an unparalleled approach to probe hydrogen dynamics and establish accurate structure-property relationships in diverse functional materials.

title: A Theoretical Investigation of Magnetic Susceptibility Measurement of Diamagnetic Liquids Using a Michelson Interferometer
abstract: We examine the theoretical use of a Michelson interferometer to infer the magnetic susceptibility of a diamagnetic liquid from a magnetically induced surface deformation. A ring magnet changes the liquid thickness along the sample beam, producing a signed phase shift relative to a fixed optical reference. For a double traversal of the sample, the fringe displacement is $m = 2(n_{\ell} - n_a)\Delta z/\lambda$. We derive the susceptibility inversion both in a local gravity approximation and with surface tension included through the linearized Young-Laplace equation. The treatment distinguishes a finite reference field from a zero-field reference, specifies the displacement sign and susceptibility contrast, and identifies calibration and uncertainty requirements. Reproducible illustrative calculations use a uniformly magnetized annulus. The results establish a theoretical measurement relation and its assumptions; they do not constitute an experimental demonstration or a verified accuracy claim.

title: An eight-channel RFSoC waveform digitizer with AC- and DC-coupled front ends and transparent dual-DDR event memory
abstract: We present Transparent Dual-DDR Event Memory (TDEM) for the triggered readout of an eight-channel radio-frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) digitizer. With either an AC- or a DC-coupled front end, each accepted trigger records 4096 samples per channel at 5 GSa/s. Two pulses 100 ns apart produced separate, overlapping records. On one DC-coupled input, interleaving calibration reduced an eight-sample periodic residual by a factor of 29 at +100 mV, but not at zero input. After a power cycle, the digitizer restored the coefficients for all eight DC-coupled inputs without a training tone. TDEM assigns complete events to 64- and 32-bit DDR4 memory interfaces in a 2:1 ratio. With this allocation alone, host page requests still determined which memory served each read. In two runs of approximately 6 s at 160 kHz, the peak receiver backlog fell from 20 140 events with the earlier readout to 1457 with event-level prefetch. Prefetch raised the sustained rate of the DC-coupled system from 150 to 170 kHz under repeated host readout pauses. With the same receiver design and a revised host buffer allocation, the AC-coupled system passed three 30 min tests at 175 kHz, each with 48 readout pauses and no rejected triggers. Without imposed pauses or background load, the host verified all 323 452 631 events in 30 min at 179.7 kHz. At 180 kHz, triggers were first rejected at the digitizer, consistent with a modelled transmitter capacity of 179.730 kHz for this event format.

title: XTCP: an open-source FPGA TCP endpoint for readout over 10 and 25 Gigabit Ethernet
abstract: XTCP is an open-source implementation of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) for high-rate detector readout. It targets sustained single-connection throughput near the TCP payload limit. In separate 10 Gigabit Ethernet transfers on the same Kintex UltraScale+ KU5P card and Linux host, XTCP and SiTCP-XG each delivered a median application-level throughput of 9.49 Gbit/s towards the host. Towards the FPGA, the medians were 9.49 Gbit/s for XTCP and 5.76 Gbit/s for the tested SiTCP-XG configuration. The XTCP prototype used more lookup tables and on-chip memory. In a 96 GiB echo test spanning repeated sequence-number wraps, recording when an acknowledgement first crossed the recovery boundary allowed four fast recoveries that the earlier signed comparison would have blocked. On one 25 Gigabit Ethernet bitstream, increasing the IP maximum transmission unit from 1500 to 9000 bytes raised median one-way throughput from 23.30 to 24.70 Gbit/s towards the host and from 22.09 to 24.08 Gbit/s towards the FPGA. At 9000 bytes these rates reached 99.7% and 97.1% of the TCP payload limit, respectively. In a separate echo test, the host verified all 8.77 TB returned by a jumbo-frame prototype over one connection in 3595 s, averaging 19.51 Gbit/s per direction.

title: A Novel Multi-Target Approach for simultaneous enhancement of brightness, intensity, and bi-spectral performance of cold neutron sources
abstract: Increasing the brightness of cold neutron beams is a central objective in modern cold neutron source development, since it largely governs the sample intensity for high-resolution neutron instruments. Raising accelerator beam power is constrained by the target heat-removal limit of 0.5-1 kW/cm2, and increasing the moderator length beyond about 20-30 cm becomes inefficient owing to the finite mean free path of cold neutrons. We propose reversing the conventional design logic: rather than tailoring the cryogenic moderator to a fixed target-premoderator source, we tailor the thermal-neutron source geometry to a high-performance moderator configuration. The concept is realized as a staircase moderator assembly of several shorter compressed moderators, each with its own target-premoderator unit, which distributes neutron production among multiple units and thus enables higher accelerator powers while preserving the brightness advantages of compressed moderators. This approach can provide additional brightness and intensity gains relative to a single low-dimensional or conventional voluminous moderator at the desired transverse beam size and may naturally generate bi-spectral neutron beams, thereby extending the dynamic range of neutron instruments.

title: High-rate accumulation of ${8.9\times10^9}$ positrons using a linac-driven buffer-gas trap combined with a SiC remoderator
authors: D. P. van der Werf (GBAR Collaboration)
abstract: We report the accumulation of $(8.9 \pm 0.9)\times10^9$ positrons in less than 35 minutes in a Penning--Malmberg trap connected to the GBAR electron-linac-based positron source. To our knowledge, this exceeds the largest previously reported trapped-positron population by more than a factor of two and was achieved at an 18-fold higher average accumulation rate of $4.5\times10^6$~e$^+$/s. The accumulated positron clouds are intended for the creation of dense positronium targets to produce keV-antihydrogen beams by charge exchange with antiprotons delivered by the CERN AD/ELENA facility. The system combines a low-energy electron linac, a modified Surko-type buffer-gas trap enhanced by a silicon carbide remoderator, and a high-field Penning--Malmberg trap operated as a positron accumulator. Time-resolved annihilation measurements provide insight into the capture and cooling dynamics, while comparisons of CO$_2$ and SF$_6$ show that the trapping signal reaches saturation at lower gas pressures with SF$_6$. Measurements show that the SiC-remoderator-based trapping scheme more than doubles the trapping efficiency, contributing to a more than threefold increase in the positron accumulation rate compared with the original configuration.

title: A muonium laser ionization system for muon acceleration studies at J-PARC
abstract: This paper reports the development and commissioning of a muonium ionization laser system installed in the H2 area of the J-PARC Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility for muon accelerator studies. In this accelerator scheme, ultraslow muons generated by laser ionization of thermal muonium atoms serve as the particle source for subsequent radio-frequency acceleration. The laser system generates coherent 122-nm pulses for muonium excitation and 355-nm pulses for photoionization of the excited muonium. A vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) pulse transport system and VUV pulse diagnostics were also developed. Muonium ionization was confirmed using a 5.7~keV muon transport line, and a muon rate of approximately 6~s$^{-1}$ was observed. These results establish operation of the ionization system and provide a platform for subsequent muon accelerator studies.

title: FGPA-based advanced muon trigger algorithms for long-lived particle detection at the High-Luminosity LHC
abstract: The CMS Level-1 trigger must reconstruct muons in real time under stringent latency and hardware resource constraints. Conventional algorithms lose efficiency for high-energy muons undergoing radiative energy losses and can be suboptimal for displaced trajectories, limiting sensitivity to exotic signatures such as long-lived particles (LLPs). The Phase-2 upgrade introduces advanced FPGAs that enable more sophisticated reconstruction algorithms. This work presents two complementary developments addressing these challenges. In the barrel region, a dedicated algorithm detects showers from Drift Tube hit patterns at the first processing stage. At the subsequent filtering stage, shower primitives are correlated with conventional trigger primitives, currently targeting radiatively showering high-momentum muons, with LLP signatures as a broader objective. Simulation studies yield approximately $80\%$ shower-classification accuracy and an estimated matching efficiency above $80\%$ for radiating muons. Firmware prototypes demonstrate a shower-detection latency of approximately $20\,\mathrm{ns}$ and sub-bunch-crossing latency for preliminary matching logic. In parallel, a hardware-oriented optimization methodology is investigated for future graph neural network based displaced-muon reconstruction in the barrel--endcap overlap region. Using a GraphSAGE proxy on a benchmark dataset, a workflow combining integer quantization, power-of-two scaling, and data-driven bit-width optimization achieves $(75.0 \pm 1.1)\%$ accuracy and a deterministic latency of $19$ cycles ($52.8\,\mathrm{ns}$ at $360\,\mathrm{MHz}$), with only $20\%$ digital signal processor utilization. These results establish a basis for implementation studies using CMS muon data.
